newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN aid agencies sound alarm bells shortages in Iraq. [CORRECTED 20:45 GMT]
newsitem.headline: UN aid agencies sound alarm bells shortages in Iraq. [CORRECTED 20:45 GMT]

text.p: U.N. aid agencies on Monday expressed alarm at the lack of food, medicine and clean water in Iraq, saying only 4 percent of the funds they asked for had been donated by the international community.

Of the $39.9 million requested in a September appeal only $1.6 million was received, from the Netherlands and from France, Yasushi Akashi, the undersecretary-general for humanitarian affairs, told a news conference.

Carol Bellamy, the director of UNICEF, the U.N. Children's Fund, said 4,500 children (corrects from 45 children) were dying each month from hunger and disease and some "modest financing" at minimum was needed in response.

And according to Catherine Bertini, director of the U.N. World Food Programme, "The humanitarian situation throughout Iraq is dismal, and with the onset of winter, will become critical for tens of thousands of women children and other Iraqis who already are living well below the poverty level."
Akashi said that one reason for the paucity of funds was the expectation that the oil-for-food plan would be go into effect shortly.

This arrangement, still to be implemented allows Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil to purchase food, medicine and other necessities in scarce supply since U.N. sanctions were imposed in August 1990.
Humanitarian goods are exempted from the embargoes but Iraq has said that the impact of sanctions on its infrastructure has added to the disastrous situation.

The latest delay came after Iraq insisted on curbing the freedom of movement for U.N. staff, limiting their numbers and choosing local personnel to work with the United Nations. Both Bertini and Bellamy said their staffs so far had encountered no difficulties.

But Akashi said Iraq's U.N. envoy, Nizar Hamdoon, told him that these issues could be resolved if the Security Council's sanctions committee would approve a new oil pricing formula under which various types of petroleum would be sold.
Iraq on Thursday submitted a new formula. Its previous one in August was approved by all committee members except the United States, which gave no reason for its delay.

The new appeal for Iraq was from October to December and would be suspended or re-examined if the oil-for-food plan were implemented, Akashi said. It was to cover more than 7 million people in all parts of Iraq.

Bertini said she needed $19 million for 2.15 million "highly vulnerable" people, including 900,000 war widows, 180,000 malnourished children under five and 200,000 pregnant or nursing mothers. UNICEF needs $10 million for essential medicine and food supplement for children suffering from disease and malnutrition.
